12:4.t: Where the Hebrew has: he wept and besought him; in Bethel he found him, and there he spoke with us, we read in the common edition: they wept and besought me, in the house of ὢν they found me, and there it was spoken to them; ὢν is interpreted sorrow. If anyone, therefore, weeps, and repents, and entreats the Lord, he will find him in the sorrow of his heart, and when he has called upon him, he will hear him answering him.

And he prevailed, he says, against the angel; and by the blessing of him whom he had overcome he was strengthened. He also wept and besought him, that is, the angel, saying: I will not let you go unless you bless me. And when, on the advice of his father and mother, he was fleeing to Mesopotamia, he found the same angel in Bethel, who spoke to him; he spoke with us, that is, in the father he spoke to the sons also, and in Jacob he loved Judah too; and from that time down to the present the memory of his name, which was imposed on him by the angel and by God, endures.

12:6.t: Since these things are so, you too, O Judah, imitate your parent: weep and beseech the Lord of hosts, and turn to him. Keep mercy and judgment, and when you have done both, hope in your God always, advancing by good works to greater things.

Therefore, O churchman, you who are called Judah, and confessing, turn daily through repentance to your Lord; and if perhaps you have sinned, imitate the prophet who says: I have labored in my groaning; every night I will wash my bed, I will water my couch with my tears. And let it not suffice to have said this, but keep the commandments of God, show mercy to others, that you yourself may obtain mercy. Judge true judgment, so that in what you judge, judgment may be passed on you. And hope in your God always, or draw near to your God continually, so that, advancing in virtue at all times, you may draw near to your God.

12:7.t: Canaan: in his hand is a deceitful balance; he has loved calumny; and Ephraim said: Yet I have become rich, I have found an idol for myself; all my labors will not find for me the iniquity which I have sinned. LXX: Canaan: in his hand is a balance of iniquity; he has loved to oppress by power; and Ephraim said: Yet I have become rich, I have found rest for myself; all his labors will not be found for him, because of the iniquities in which he has sinned. He had admonished Judah to turn to the Lord his God, and to keep mercy and judgment, and to hope in the Lord always, or to draw near to him continually. Now the discourse turns to Ephraim, that is, to the ten tribes, whom he calls Canaan, according to what Daniel says to the elder, who was certainly of the seed of Judah: Seed of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you. And in Ezekiel we read it said to Jerusalem: Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite. […]

Hence this very thing is also referred to the heretics. For Canaan can be interpreted: as if moving. And note that he said: as if moving, not moving. They are moving those whom they have deceived; as if moving, those whom they have tempted. But because these are founded upon the rock, they can be shaken by no whirlwind, nor change the footprint of their feet. In the hand of a Canaan of this sort, that is, in his works, there is a deceitful and unjust balance; for whatever the heretic speaks does not have the justice of God, and is full of deceit and frauds; whence they also love calumny, while they press down the innocent, or oppress them by power.

12:8.t: And lest we should think that some other Canaan is to be understood, he states more plainly who this Canaan is. Ephraim said: Yet I have become rich; and the sense is: it makes no difference whence I possess it, so long as I possess it. Very many suffer from this disease, of whom it is written: Riches gathered unjustly will be vomited up. For the ransom of a man's soul is his own riches. Hence we are commanded to make ourselves friends of the unrighteous mammon, who can receive us into the eternal tabernacles. But Ephraim, who glories and says: Yet I have become rich, I have found an idol for myself, or ἀνωφελὲς, that is, auen, which does not profit its possessor, has sweated with vain labor. Just as the belly is god to the glutton and the luxurious, so the avaricious man too worships the idol of gold, and says in his heart: I have found what I was seeking; but he will hear: Fool, this night your soul will be snatched from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be? […]

The poor churchman is oppressed by the wordiness and the subtleties of the heretics, who, after they have deceived some, are accustomed to say: we have become rich, we have a very great multitude; a crowd of disciples follows us; we have found an idol, or refreshment, for ourselves. For heresies are put together chiefly for this reason, that they may devour the houses of widows, who are always learning and never arrive at the knowledge of the truth. And beautifully: I have found, he says, an idol for myself. For all the fictions of the heretics are idols and images of the Gentiles; nor do they differ much in impiety, though they seem to differ in name. And they are accustomed to say: whatever I do, whatever I perform, cannot be imputed to me; for I have my riches, the arguments of the philosophers; I have a multitude of people, and whoever beholds it will not think that I sin.

12:9.t: And I am the Lord your God from the land of Egypt; I will yet make you sit in tabernacles as in the days of festivity; and I have spoken upon the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and in the hand of the prophets I have been likened. LXX: But I am the Lord your God, I brought you out of the land of Egypt; I will yet make you dwell in tabernacles, as in the days of solemnity, and I will speak to the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and in the hands of the prophets I have been likened. You indeed have sinned so greatly that you rejoiced in crime, and thought the multitude of your sins to be riches, and said: I have become rich, I have found an idol for myself; all my labors will not be able to find my sins. But I, the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt when you were serving Pharaoh and building cities of mud and straw, still grant you room for repentance, and by the greatness of my promises I exhort you to return to me; […]

To those also who have been led astray by the heretics it is said that they should return to the Lord, who prefers the repentance of the sinner to his death; for he is the one who brought them out of the land of Egypt, that is, out of the darkness and error of the Gentiles. And lest perhaps, remembering their sin, they should return too slowly: I will yet, he says, make you sit in tabernacles, as in the days of festivity; so that what baptism does, repentance may do, and they may dwell in the tabernacles of the Savior, that is, in the Churches, of which it is said: Planted in the house of the Lord, they will flourish in the courts of the house of our God.

12:10.t: For certain of these men used to see the prophetic Spirit and His active influences poured forth for all kinds of gifts; others, again, [beheld] the advent of the Lord, and that dispensation which obtained from the beginning, by which He accomplished the will of the Father with regard to things both celestial and terrestrial; and others [beheld] paternal glories adapted to the times, and to those who saw and who heard them then, and to all who were subsequently to hear them. Thus, therefore, was God revealed; for God the Father is shown forth through all these [operations], the Spirit indeed working, and the Son ministering, while the Father was approving, and man's salvation being accomplished. As He also declares through Hosea the prophet: "I," He says, "have multiplied visions, and have used similitudes by the ministry of the prophets." But the apostle expounded this very passage, when he said, "Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are differences of ministrations, but the same Lord; […]

But that both the apostles and their disciples thus taught as the Church preaches, and thus teaching were perfected, wherefore also they were called away to that which is perfect-Stephen, teaching these truths, when he was yet on earth, saw the glory of God, and Jesus on His right hand, and exclaimed, "Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing on the right hand of God." These words he said, and was stoned; and thus did he fulfil the perfect doctrine, copying in every respect the Leader of martyrdom, and praying for those who were slaying him, in these words: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." Thus were they perfected who knew one and the same God, who from beginning to end was present with mankind in the various dispensations; as the prophet Hosea declares: "I have filled up visions, and used similitudes by the hands of the prophets."

For it is I who through all the prophets and various kinds of visions have been likened to men, and have called you to repentance. Is it not of human likeness when Moses, raising his hands on high, prays that Joshua may conquer Amalek, and the mysteries of the cross are shown in him? Is not God likened in the hands of the prophets when Jonah is in the deep three days and nights, that he may signify the Lord rising from the underworld on the third day? And we read of visions multiplied in all the prophets, when Ezekiel sees God sitting like a charioteer above the cherubim. And Isaiah: I saw, he says, the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, and two seraphim around him crying to one another: holy, holy, holy, Lord God Sabaoth. And Habakkuk stood on his watchtower, to see horns in the hands of the Savior, in which his strength is hidden. Hence the psalmist too cries out: I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me. […]

And lest they think that the heresiarchs and leaders of their error have spoken by the spirit of God: it is I, he says, who spoke to the prophets, and not to your masters; I multiplied visions, and in the hand of my prophets, who are established in the Church, I have been likened.

12:11.t: If Gilead is an idol, then in vain were they sacrificing to oxen in Gilgal; for their altars too are like heaps upon the furrows of the field. LXX: If Gilead is not, then the princes sacrificing in Gilgala were false, and their altars like tortoises upon the desert of the field. Where we have translated 'to oxen', which in Hebrew are called surim, the LXX translated 'princes', who are called sarim, deceived by the likeness and ambiguity of the word. Again, where we have put 'heaps', which in Hebrew are called gallim and properly signify θῖνας, that is, mounds gathered together out of sand, which, chiefly in the desert and on the shores, are either increased or diminished as the wind blows, the LXX translated 'tortoises', for which Symmachus rendered 'heaps of stones', Theodotion 'hills'. And indeed, if you look at θῖνας, they have the likeness of great tortoises in a desert field, or on banks and shores, rising a little above the ground. […]

12:12.t: Jacob fled into the country of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept watch. But by a prophet the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved. LXX: And Jacob withdrew into the plain of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he guarded; and by a prophet the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet he was preserved. It seems that, without reason and without prophetic order, after the idol of Gilead and Gilgal and the altars like heaps of stones, he suddenly chose to narrate the history of Genesis concerning Jacob; which is at once resolved by one who remembers having read above concerning Jacob: In the womb he supplanted his brother, and in his strength he was made upright with the angel; and he prevailed over the angel and was strengthened; he wept and besought him: in Bethel he found him, and there he spoke with us. This Jacob, therefore, was not strengthened by the angel in vain; […]

He will not err who says that Jacob the supplanter, and Israel who sees the Lord, went before as a type of the Lord; and that Rachel, at first barren and beautiful, whom Jacob loved most, signifies the Church; but that Leah, with bleary eyes and fruitful, shows the mysteries of the Synagogue; and that he himself led the people of believers out of the darkness of this world, and came to the sweetest streams of the Jordan, that is, of baptism.

12:13.t: And because he had once said both Jacob and Israel, he joins the father and the sons, and recalls the history that follows, when by the prophet Moses the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt, and the twelve tribes which were begotten of Israel were preserved, as the prophet led them out.

12:14.t: Ephraim provoked me to anger in his bitternesses, and his blood will come upon him, and his reproach his Lord will restore to him. LXX: likewise. Since, then, I had bestowed such great things on Ephraim that I brought him back rich and a lord, and the parent of many sons, who had been naked and an exile and alone, Ephraim deserted me, nay, provoked me to anger; and by his bitterness he made me bitter, who am sweet. Hence his blood will come upon him, that is: he himself will be the cause of his own death, according to what David says to the man who announced the death of Saul and related that the king of Israel had been slain by him: Your blood be upon your head. Not by my sentence, but by the blood of Saul will your blood be shed. […]

13:1.t: But when the heretics speak, nay, the princes of the heretics, that is, Ephraim, horror and trembling will seize the unhappy people; and he will sin in the idols which he has fashioned from his own heart, and he dies with the people whom he has seduced.

When Ephraim spoke, horror seized Israel, and he sinned in Baal, and died; and now they have added to sinning, and have made for themselves a molten image of their silver, as it were the likeness of idols; the whole is the work of craftsmen; to these they themselves say: Sacrifice men, adoring calves. LXX: According to the word of Ephraim he himself received justifications in Israel, and placed them for Baal, and died; and now he has added that he might sin, and they made for themselves a molten image of their silver, after the image of idols, molten works of craftsmen; to these they themselves say: Sacrifice men, for the calves have failed. Where the LXX translated: sacrifice men, for the calves have failed, and we rendered: sacrifice men, adoring calves, Symmachus translated: sacrifice; let men adore calves; so that the sense is: Sacrifice, that is, offer sacrifice to idols, and let the pause fall up to this point; then: let men, a rational animal, adore calves, dumb living creatures. […]

13:2.t: And it is not enough for him to have fallen, unless he turns the tongue which he had received for singing of God into images of idols, and with artful eloquence composes a dogma like the truth, which is nothing else but a contrivance of human depravity. And they instruct their disciples that they too should sacrifice men, that is, steal them from the Church of God and bring them in to the heretics, and kill those whom they have deceived. What follows: For the calves have failed, has this sense: Do not seek those whom you may seduce among the Gentiles, who are called brute animals; but seize those, sacrifice those, who, set within the Church, are reckoned by the name of Christ and are called men, according to that prophetic word: But choice foods.

13:3.t: Therefore they will be like a morning cloud, and like the morning dew passing away, like dust snatched by the whirlwind from the threshing floor, and like smoke from the chimney. LXX: likewise; changing only this, which is at the end: and like vapor from locusts, or from tears, because in most manuscripts we find ἀκρίδων (of locusts) set down, in others δακρύων (of tears). Because, he says, they sacrificed men in place of calves, and adored calves, therefore they will be like a morning cloud, and like the dew passing away in the morning, like dust snatched by the whirlwind from the threshing floor, and like smoke from the chimney. All these are seen for a time and suddenly vanish, according to what he had said: Samaria has made her king pass away like foam upon the face of the water. And again: As the morning passes, the king of Israel will pass away. […]

13:4.t: For through the Lord Christ all things were created; and therefore it is His proper name that He should be the Creator. Does not both the reality and the title of His creative power belong to Him? Melchisedec is our witness, thus declaring God to be Creator of heaven and earth: "Blessed be Abraham of God most high, Who created heaven and earth." The prophet Hosea also is witness, saying, "I am the Lord thy God, that establish the heavens and create the earth, Whose hands have created all the host of heaven." Peter too is witness, writing thus, "Committing your souls as to a faithful Creator." Why do we apply the name of the work to the Maker of that work? Why do we give the same name to God and to our fellowmen? He is our Creator, He is the Creator of all the heavenly host.

But I am the Lord your God from the land of Egypt. In place of which one reads in the LXX: But I am the Lord your God ÷ who make firm the heaven and create the earth, whose hand created all the host of heaven, and I did not show them to you, that you might walk after them. : And I brought you out of the land of Egypt. Since these words are not found in the Hebrew, and are rendered by none of the translators, and are not read in the ancient edition of the LXX either, they must be marked beforehand with an obelus; especially since their sense is plain. Let us therefore pass on to the rest, joining the preceding section to what follows:

But I am the Lord your God from the land of Egypt, and you shall know no God besides me, and there is no savior but me.

I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of solitude, according to their pastures; and they were filled and were satisfied; they lifted up their heart and forgot me. LXX: But I am the Lord your God, and I brought you out of the land of Egypt; and you shall know no God but me, and there is no savior besides me. I was pasturing you in the desert, in an uninhabitable land, according to their pastures; and they were filled to satiety, and their hearts were lifted up; therefore they forgot me. He who had said above: Jacob fled into the region of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept watch; […]

The heretics too the Lord brought out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage, and out of the iron furnace, who at first served King Pharaoh and his captains; and he commanded them in the Church to know no other God except him who is the creator of all things and knows how to save those whom he made.

13:5.t: I, who am the founder of all things, knew you, or fed you, in the wilderness and in an uninhabitable land, where there is want of all things, where there are no waters; I gave you manna from heaven, and brought forth springs of water from the hardest rock. And they, according to what is written elsewhere: The beloved grew fat, became thick, grew broad, and kicked, now also have eaten and been satisfied, and have lifted up their heart, and have forgotten him whose benefits they ought to have remembered. For through so great a waste of desert, where not only no crops and trees and vines, but not even grass is produced, and no waters temper the heat of the sun, Israel could not for forty years have reached the land of the Jordan, unless the Lord had provided everything.

He himself knew them and fed them in the land of solitude, so that they could say: The Lord pastures me and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture there he has set me, he has brought me up beside the water of refreshment. And he gave them the bread of angels, manna from heaven, which they had never eaten in Egypt, and water from the rock that followed them. Now the rock, according to the Apostle, is Christ; and they ate and were filled, and did not endure the food of the Lord. To them the same Apostle says: Already you are satisfied, already you have become rich; without us you reign, and would that you did reign, so that we too might reign with you. For they ate in the holy Scriptures the bread that came down from heaven, and said with David: The uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom you have made manifest to me. […]

13:7.t: I know Him, Who, though free from passion, meets us like a bear robbed of her whelps, like a leopard in the way of the Assyrians, not only those of that day, but if anyone now is an Assyrian in wickedness: nor is it possible to escape the might and speed of His wrath when He watches over our impieties, and His jealousy, which knoweth to devour His adversaries, pursues His enemies to the death.

And I will be to them like a lioness, like a leopard on the way of the Assyrians; I will meet them like a bear robbed of her cubs, and I will tear apart the inner parts of their liver; and I will devour them there like a lion; the beast of the field will rend them. LXX: And I will be to them like a panther and like a leopard on the way of the Assyrians; I will meet them like a bear in want of food, and I will tear apart the inner parts of their heart; and the whelps of the forests will devour them there, the beasts of the field will tear them apart. They were filled and satisfied; they lifted up their hearts and forgot me. But I, he says, will be to them like a lioness, or a panther, of which we spoke more fully above; and like a leopard on the way of the Assyrians, when they are led captive by the Assyrians; and I will meet them like a bear robbed of her cubs, or in want of food; and I will tear apart all their vital organs. […]

13:9.t: You have become a surfeit to me: I will by no means forgive your sins. For which Aquila translated, I have labored in bearing; Symmachus ἐκοπώθην ἱλασκόμενος, that is, I have grown weary of showing mercy; to show that he will by no means have mercy any longer, because it is one thing to kill the servants sent to them, another to kill the Son. This sense we read also in the prophet Hosea: Your destruction, O Israel; only in me is your help (Hos 13:9). Which is understood thus: You would perish, Israel, because you are saved not by your own merit but only by my help.

Your destruction, Israel; only in me is your help. Where is your king? Now above all they save you in all your cities; and your judges, of whom you said: Give me a king and princes; I will give you a king in my fury, and I will take him away in my indignation. LXX: Who will help your corruption, Israel? Where is this king of yours? And let him save you in all your cities; let him judge you, of whom you said: Give me a king and a prince; and I gave you a king and a prince, and I gave you a king in my anger, and I held him in my fury. Where the LXX translated I held, all the others rendered I took away. Unhappy Israel, and worthy of a perpetual curse, which has gone down into so great a depth of impiety that it is saved by the mercy of God alone! But in the Hebrew it can also be read in this sense: May you perish, Israel, because nothing is left to you except to be preserved by my clemency alone. In the LXX, however, the sense is different: Who will help your corruption, Israel? […]

Every heretic is lost and given over to corruption; for whoever corrupts the temple of God, the Lord will destroy him; and he has help in nothing else but in the mercy of God alone, which he obtains by repentance.

13:10.t: Where is your king, of whom you said to Samuel: Appoint a king over us to judge us, as the other nations also have. And when he spoke against it, you answered: By no means; but there shall be a king over us, and we too shall be like all the nations, and our king will judge us, and go out before us, and fight for us. Let him, then, of whom you had promised yourself that he would fight your wars, now come to your aid in your need, and free all your cities from servitude. Where are your judges? Where are your kings? For you said: Give me a king and princes; and so I gave you Saul as king in my fury, so much so that in the days of harvest I displayed rain, contrary to the nature of the province of Judea. And I took away, he says, the king in my indignation, namely Zedekiah, so that the one I had given with fury I might take away with indignation. Others think that the king given in fury was Jeroboam son of Nebat, and the one taken away in indignation Hoshea, the last king of the ten tribes. […]

His king and judges are the devil and the demons, or all the princes of perverse dogmas, who will not be able to free them in the time of need and distress, who were given in fury and will be taken away in indignation; not that the Lord wished them to have such kings, otherwise he would not take away those whom he had given of his own accord, but because he let them go after their own wills, so that, eating, and with their flesh grown fat, they might be nauseated and vomit it out through their nostrils, and begin to hate those whom they followed with such zeal.

13:11.t: But let no one who suffers such a ruler, blame him whom he suffers: because his being subject to the power of a wicked ruler was doubtless of his own desert. Let him therefore rather blame the fault of his own evil doings, than the injustice of his ruler. For it is written, "I will give thee kings in Mine anger." Why then do we scorn their being set over us, whose authority over us we endure from the anger of the Lord? If then we receive rulers, according to our deserts, from the wrath of God, we infer from their conduct, what to think in our estimate of ourselves. Although even the Elect are frequently placed under the reprobate. Whence also David for a long time endured Saul. But it is proved by the subsequent sin of adultery, that he then deserved to be thus heavily oppressed by the cruelty of him who was set over him.
13:11.s: Morals on the Book of Job, Book 25:34

13:12.t: The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is hidden; the pains of a woman in labor will come upon him; he is an unwise son; for now he will not stand in the crushing of the children. LXX: A gathering of iniquity is Ephraim; his sin is hidden; pains as of a woman in labor will come upon him; this is your wise son, because now he will not hold out in the crushing of the children. Just as, if something is bound up in a bag, it is kept, and is not lost to him for whom it was tied up, so every iniquity by which Ephraim has sinned against God is bound up for him, and is reserved, hidden as in a purse. Finally, when the day of vengeance has come, and the final captivity, pains as of a woman in labor will come upon him, or will seize him. A woman in labor knows long before she gives birth, from the time she conceived, that she is going to give birth, and daily awaits the extreme torments and agonies that are to come. […]

13:14.t: Now the laws of love summoned Him even as far as Death and the dead themselves, so that He might summon the souls of those who were long time dead. And so because He cared for the salvation of all for ages past, and that "He might bring to naught him that hath the power of death," as Scripture teaches, here again he underwent the dispensation in His mingled Natures: as Man, he left His Body to the usual burial, while as God He departed from it. For He cried with a loud cry, and said to the Father: "I commend my spirit," and departed from the body free, in no wise waiting for death, who was lagging as it were in fear to come to Him; nay, rather, He pursued him from behind and drove him on, trodden under His feet and fleeing, and He burst the eternal gates of his dark realms, and made a road of return back again to life for the dead there bound with the bonds of death. […]
13:14.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 4, Chapter 12

13:14.t: No one could know Wisdom; for no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him. Therefore, He Himself revealed to John with whom Wisdom was; and for this reason, he said, not as his own, but what Wisdom had infused in him: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God. Wisdom does not know destruction, it does not know wickedness. For destruction could not hold it, who said: Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?
13:14.s: The Prayer of Job and David 1:9.31

13:14.t: From the hand of death I will free them, from death I will redeem them. I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell. Consolation is hidden from my eyes, because he divides between brothers. LXX: From the hand of hell I will free them, from death I will redeem them; where is your cause, death? Where is your sting, hell? Consolation is hidden from my eyes, because he will divide between brothers. According to both understandings, both of Ephraim, that is, of the ten tribes, and of the heretics, who could not hold out in the crushing of their children when the pains as of a woman in labor came, the Lord promises that he will free them from the hand of death and redeem them from death. Now he calls the hand of death the works by which it kills, according to what is written: Death and life are in the hand of the tongue. And the Lord freed all and redeemed them in the passion of the cross and the shedding of his blood, when his soul went down into hell and his flesh did not see corruption; […]

And seeing the hard necessity of death, and that there is no man who lives and does not see death, the most merciful Father remembers the ancient sentence, that in Adam we all die. Or the prophet, understanding his own frailty and the condition of human flesh: Consolation, he says, is hidden from my eyes; and the sense is: I am not able to be consoled; whatever I conceive in my mind cannot soften my grief, as I see names most dear to one another severed by death; hell itself, he says, divides between brothers. Whatever, then, separates brothers is to be called hell; and above all the harlot woman, who, calling the unwise man to herself, says in the wealth of prudence: Touch gladly the hidden loaves, and the sweetness of stolen water; and the unwise man does not know that the earth-born perish with her and run into the depth of hell. For whatever is not permitted is desired the more, and what is sweet through rarity is turned into bitterness through constancy. […]

Still I think it right to convict them plainly of foolishly resisting the inspired Scriptures, and to show that they completely mistook the sense of what the sacred writings teach. For come and let us see what the company of the holy prophets has spoken to us upon this point, and what are the declarations which the Lord of hosts has made by their means. He said therefore of those that sleep, "I will deliver them from the hand of the grave; I will redeem them from death: Where is your condemnation, O death? O grave, where is your sting?" Now what is meant by the condemnation of death, and by its sting also, the blessed Paul has taught us, saying, "But the sting of death is sin: and the strength of sin is the law." For he compares death to a scorpion, the sting of which is sin: for by its poison it slays the soul. And the law, he says, was the strength of sin: for so he himself again elsewhere protests, saying, "I had not known sin but by the law:" "for where there is no law, there is no transgression of the law." […]
13:14.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

13:14.t: For God’s mercy towards us is the more wonderful that Christ died not for the righteous nor for the holy, but for the unrighteous and wicked; and though the nature of the Godhead could not sustain the sting of death, yet at His birth He took from us that which He might offer for us. For of old He threatened our death with the power of His death, saying by the mouth of Hosea the prophet, “O death, I will be thy death, and I will be thy destruction, O hell.” For by dying He underwent the laws of hell, but by rising again He broke them, and so destroyed the continuity of death as to make it temporal instead of eternal. “For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.”

Yet again the same prophet says: From the power of the grave will I ransom them. Where is thy victory, O death! Where is thy sting, O grave!—a passage which the Apostle has used concerning the resurrection.

From this solemnity indeed the example of resurrection was given to us, the hope of the heavenly homeland was opened, and the glory of the supernal kingdom was made something we might already anticipate. Through this, the elect, who although they were in the bosom of tranquility, were nevertheless held in the confines of hell, were led back to the delights of paradise. What the Lord said before His passion, He fulfilled in His resurrection: "If I am lifted up from the earth," He said, "I will draw all things to myself." For He drew all things, He who left none of His elect in the underworld. He took away all things—that is, all the elect. For He did not restore to pardon by rising again any unbelievers or those consigned to eternal punishments for their crimes; but He snatched from the confines of hell those whom He recognized as His own in faith and in deeds. Whence rightly also He says through Hosea: "I will be your death, O death; I will be your sting, O hell." […]

Whence rightly also He says through Hosea: "I will be your death, O death; I will be your sting, O hell." For what we kill, we cause to exist no more entirely. But from what we bite, we take away a part and leave a part behind. Therefore, because in His elect He utterly killed death, He became the death of death. But because He took away a part from hell and left a part behind, He did not utterly kill but bit hell. Therefore He says: "I will be your death, O death." As if He were saying openly: Because in my elect I utterly destroy you, I will be your death; I will be your sting, O hell, because when they have been taken away, I pierce you in part. What then is this solemnity which destroyed the confines of hell and opened to us the gates of the heavenly kingdom?

We have been brought to life in Christ through Christ, because Christ triumphed over death: whence death could not swallow him up, but rather the font of life swallowed up death, according to what was said: "I will be your death, O death." In no other way could we be healed and saved.

13:15.t: The Lord will bring a burning wind rising from the desert, and it will dry up its veins, and lay waste its spring, and he will plunder the treasure of every desirable vessel. LXX: The Lord will bring a burning wind from the desert upon them, and will dry up its veins, and lay waste its springs; he will parch its land and all the desirable vessels. I have read in the commentaries of a certain writer that the burning wind which the Lord will bring from the desert is the one that struck the house of Job at its four corners and made it fall upon his sons as they feasted, and that it is one of those winds which we read in the Gospel blow and come with whirlwind, rains and floods to overturn the house that is built upon the rock, or upon the sand. This by no means seems right to me; for it is not written in Job that the Lord brought the wind from the desert; […]

13:16.t: Let Samaria perish, because she has provoked her God to bitterness; let them perish by the sword; let their little ones be dashed and her pregnant women be ripped open. LXX: Samaria will be destroyed, because she has resisted her God; they will perish by the sword, and let their sucklings be dashed against the rock, and those with child be torn apart. We have often said that the ten tribes are called Samaria from the capital city Samaria, which is now called Augusta, that is, Sebaste, from the name of Augustus. And why the city was called Samaria we read in the book of Kings. The prophet, then, commands, and, to speak more truly, speaks in the optative mood, that Samaria should perish. For though God was preparing such great goods for her, she acts against God and follows rather the images of demons. […]

14:1.t: Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have fallen in your iniquity. Take words with you, and return to the Lord; say to him: Take away all iniquity and receive the good, and we will render the calves of our lips. Assyria will not save us, we will not mount upon a horse; nor will we say any more: Our gods, the works of our hands; for you will have mercy on the orphan who is in you. LXX: Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have been weakened in your iniquities; take words with you and turn back to the Lord, say to him, so that you may not take up iniquity, but may receive good things; and we will render the fruit of our lips. Assyria will not save us, we will not mount upon a horse; by no means will we say any more: Our gods, to the works of our hands; he who is in you will have mercy on the orphan. Now that Samaria and its men are perishing, and its little ones and pregnant women have been slain, dashed down and ripped open, all Israel is called to repentance; […]

To every perverse dogma also the prophet speaks daily, and calls its followers to repentance, saying: Return to the Lord your God, you who have fallen, or have grown weak, having lost the health of the Lord; take words with you, the true confession of faith, and say: Take away the iniquity that dwells in our heart, and receive the good of faith. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. The calves and victims, or the fruit of the lips, are to believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and in the passion and resurrection of the Lord; and whoever has offered this to him will by no means hope in the Assyrian king, of whom we have often spoken. Nor will he mount upon the horse which the Lord commands by no means to be multiplied, the horse with which Pharaoh was drowned together with his cavalry. For every heretic, through pride, mounts horses which he himself has bred in his error. […]

14:2.t: Take, he says, words with you, that is, prayers and the confession of sins, and return to the Lord as much by words as by works; and say to him: Take away all iniquity, leave in us nothing of our sickness and of our former ruin, lest the revived seedlings of an evil seed sprout again; and receive, he says, the good. For unless you take away our evils, we cannot have a good to offer you, according to what is written elsewhere: Turn away from evil and do good; and we will render, he says, the calves of our lips. For the calves, which in Hebrew are called pharim, the Seventy translated fruit, which is called pheri, through the likeness of a deceptive word. But the calves of the lips are praises to God and thanksgiving: For a sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit. Therefore, fleshly victims being already rejected at that time, the offering acceptable to God is pure confession.

A SHIP is guided to the right port by means of the helm; but the word of God pilots the soul of man, and leads him without risk of error to every thing that is necessary for salvation. For so spoke one of the holy prophets; "Take with you words:" even those which are inspired by the Holy Spirit: for no man of sense will say, that it means the words of the wise of this world. For their words lead men unto the pit of destruction, by bringing polytheism into the world, and by inciting unto carnal pleasure, and to the desire of the world's vain distractions: but the words of God point out the pathway to a better life, and beget in us an earnestness which makes us cheerfully advance unto the duty of performing all those things, by means of which we are made partakers of eternal life.
14:2.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

14:2.t: I HEAR one of the holy prophets trying to win unto repentance those who are far from God, and saying, "Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God: for you have become weak in your iniquity. Take with you words, and return to the Lord our God." What sort of words then did he, under the influence of the Spirit, command them to take with them? Or were they not such as become those who wish to repent; such namely, as would appease God, Who is gentle, and loves mercy. For He even said by one of the holy prophets, "Return you returning children, and I will heal your breaches." And yet again by the voice of Ezekiel, "Return you altogether from your wickednesses, O house of Israel. Cast away from you all your iniquities which you have committed, that they be not to you for a punishment of iniquity. For I have no pleasure in the death of the sinner, as that he should turn from his evil way and live." […]
14:2.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

14:3.t: Those who say that they will render the calves of the lips, and will sing the praises of God with unceasing voice, also promise something else: that they will by no means have hope in the Assyrians, nor upon Egyptian horses, because a horse is deceptive for safety, and that they will no longer worship the works of their hands, the golden calves which they cast in Dan and Bethel; and therefore they say: By no means will we say to the work of our hands: our gods, for you will have mercy on the orphan who is in you; that is, on the people of Israel, of whom you had said: Israel is my firstborn son. And: I have begotten sons and exalted them, but they have despised me. And in another place: Foreign sons have lied to me. Now he is called an orphan because he has lost God as his father. A certain writer has explained the orphan as him who has withdrawn from an evil father, the devil, and who is therefore lifted up by the mercy of God.

14:4.t: I will heal their breaches, I will love them freely, for my fury is turned away from him; I will be like the dew. Israel will spring up like the lily, and his root will break forth like that of Lebanon; his branches will spread, and his glory will be like the olive, and his fragrance like that of Lebanon. Those who sit in his shade will be converted, they will live on wheat and will spring up like the vine. His memorial like the wine of Lebanon. Ephraim, what more have I to do with idols? I will hear him and direct him; I, like a green fir tree; from me your fruit has been found. LXX: I will heal their dwellings; I will love them openly, for my anger is turned away from them; I will be like the dew. Israel will flower like the lily and will send out his roots like Lebanon; his branches will spread, and he will be like a fruitful olive, and his fragrance like that of Lebanon; they will turn back and sit under his shade; […]

Whatever we have interpreted according to ἀναγωγὴν (anagogy) of the coming of the Lord the Savior and of the conversion of the true Israel, this can be referred as much to heretics and Jews as to the Gentiles and to every perverse dogma, so that when they have repented they may obtain pardon. If, therefore, the fullness of the promise was fulfilled at the coming of the Savior, and is fulfilled daily in the Church, we must believe that it will be fulfilled more fully when, perfection having come, what is now in part will be done away. We must note what we have often said: that the salvation of Israel and of the return to God, and the redemption from captivity, are to be taken not carnally, as the Jews think, but spiritually, as is most truly proved.

14:5.t: This is our Faith. Thus did God will that He should be known by all, thus believed the three children, and felt not the fire into the midst whereof they were cast, which destroyed and burnt up unbelievers, whilst it fell harmless as dew upon the faithful, for whom the flames kindled by others became cold, seeing that the torment had justly lost its power in conflict with faith. For with them there was One in the form of an angel, comforting them, to the end that in the number of the Trinity one Supreme Power might be praised. God was praised, the Son of God was seen in God's angel, holy and spiritual grace spake in the children.

And I will be to them like the dew; so that with my dew I may quench the Babylonian furnace and the oven of the blazing fire, I who also through the patriarch Isaac spoke to my servant Jacob: Of the dew of heaven shall your dwelling be. For just as the Lord becomes to believers light, way, truth, bread, vine, fire, shepherd, lamb, door, worm, and the rest; so for us who need his mercy, and burn with the fevers of sins, he is turned into dew, he to whom Isaiah says: For the dew that is from you is their health. And in the song of Deuteronomy Moses speaks: Let my words descend like the dew. And when the Lord has sprinkled us with his dew, and has watered the dryness of our breast with his rains, we will spring up, nay, we will flower like the lily, imitating the Lord the Savior, who says in the Song of Songs: I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys; and he speaks to his bride, who has no wrinkle or spot: As the lily in the midst of thorns, so is my nearest one in the midst of the daughters. […]

14:6.t: The branches of these trees stretch this way and that, so that the birds of heaven may come and dwell in them. And lest perhaps we should think, because he had said: his root will break forth, or: he will send out his roots like Lebanon, that he was speaking of cedars and unfruitful trees, he compares the holy man, converted to the Lord, to the fruit-bearing olive, the man who says in another place: But I am like a fruitful olive in the house of God. Its fruit the five wise virgins prepared for themselves; by it the swelling of wounds is soothed, the limbs of the sick find rest, light is kindled in darkness, those who contend in the contest are anointed. This olive will have a fragrance like that of Lebanon, or of frankincense, which is a kind of incense: ὁμωνύμως (by the same name) among the Greeks and the Hebrews both the mountain and frankincense are so called; […]

14:7.t: But those who have been converted to the Lord will receive the reward of their conversion, that they may sit in his shade and say: Under his shade I rested and sat, and his fruit is sweet in my mouth. And when they have sat in his shade, those who before had been dead will live; or, according to the Seventy, they will drink and be inebriated with wheat, that is, with an abundance of all things. That inebriation here signifies not the overturning of the mind but a plenty of all things, that little verse declares, saying: You have visited the earth and inebriated it. And the banquet of Joseph, at which he is said to have inebriated his brothers. And the Lord, speaking to the apostles: Eat, friends, and drink, and be inebriated, brothers. Or, because the Lord himself is the grain and the vine, whoever believes in him is said to be inebriated. Finally there follows: And it will flower like the vine, his memorial like the wine of Lebanon. […]

14:8.t: Since, therefore, so great an abundance of all things is to come, O Ephraim, everyone who repents and who has begun to be mine, put away idols, despise images; for I am he who humbled you, and I will exalt you; or, I will hear and direct, and I will make him like a green fir tree, so that of him it may be said in the psalm, according to the Hebrews: The fir tree is its house. Or at least, I will be like a dense juniper, so that he may rest under my shade. Of ἀρκεύθοις, that is, of junipers, according to the Seventy translators, Solomon is recorded to have made the doors of the temple, because Christ, through whom we come to the Father, has this nature, that he always flowers, always bears new fruits, and never lays aside his greenness. This juniper, for those who rest under its shade, so that they may not be struck by the burning of this world and the heat may not strike their head, as it once struck Jonah's too, gives fruits, and provides not only rest to those who sleep and sit, but also fullness to those who eat.

14:9.t: And to such a degree does the gospel desire that there should be wise people among believers, that for the sake of exercising the understanding of its hearers, it has spoken certain truths in enigmas, others in what are called "dark" sayings, others in parables, and others in problems. And one of the prophets—Hosea—says at the end of his prophecy, "Who is wise, and he will understand these things? Or prudent, and he shall know them?"

Who is wise, and will understand these things? Understanding, and will know these things? For the ways of the Lord are right, and the just will walk in them, but transgressors will fall in them. LXX: Who is wise, and will understand these things, or understanding, and will know them? For the ways of the Lord are right, and the just will walk in them; but those who are impious will be weakened in them. When he says: Who is wise, and will understand these things? understanding, and will know them? he shows the obscurity of the book and the difficulty of its explanation. But if he himself who wrote it confesses that it is either difficult or impossible, what can we do, who, with bleary eyes darkened by the filth of sins, cannot gaze upon the brightest radiance of the sun, except say what is written: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! […]
